info.name: Restful Booker - Manual API Testing Practice
info.description:
# Restful Booker - Manual API Testing Practice

A **manual** API testing course and test suite for the public **Restful Booker** practice API (https://restful-booker.herokuapp.com/apidoc/index.html).

- **129 requests in 19 folders.** Every request is a fully documented test case: open its **Docs** tab.
- **Manual only.** There are no scripts, no automatic assertions and no automatic variable extraction. You send each request, inspect the response, record the result and copy values (booking ID, token) into the environment yourself.
- **Start with folder 00**: its **Overview** tab explains setup, golden rules and how expected results are written.

## Quick start

1. Import this collection and `Restful-Booker-Environment.postman_environment.json`.
2. Select **Restful Booker Environment** in the environment selector (top right).
3. Run **00.01** (expect `201 Created`), then **01.01 → 01.03**.

## Chapters

| Folder | Requests |
|---|---|
| 00 - Introduction and Health Check | 1 |
| 01 - API Fundamentals and Request Anatomy | 3 |
| 02 - HTTP Methods | 7 |
| 03 - Status Codes | 5 |
| 04 - Headers and Content Types | 6 |
| 05 - Query and Path Parameters | 13 |
| 06 - JSON and Request Body | 8 |
| 07 - Authentication | 5 |
| 08 - Authorization | 7 |
| 09 - API Contracts and Response Validation | 4 |
| 10 - Positive Testing | 7 |
| 11 - Negative Testing | 10 |
| 12 - Boundary Testing | 12 |
| 13 - Business Validation | 9 |
| 14 - Test Case Design | 4 |
| 15 - API Chaining | 5 |
| 16 - CRUD Workflow | 9 |
| 17 - End-to-End Booking Flow | 10 |
| 18 - Cleanup and Reusable Requests | 4 |

## Variables (environment only)

`base_url`, `username`, `password` are pre-filled with the documented public demo values. `booking_id` and `token` start empty: **you** fill them by copying values from responses.

## Expected results

**Documented** expectations come from the official documentation. Where the documentation is silent, a test is marked **Not documented - investigate** and states the convention or business rule used as the oracle. Optional *mentor notes* describe behaviour observed on a local build of the official restful-booker source (commit 0046115, March 2026). The public instance may differ, so always record what **you** observe.

## Safety

Work only on bookings you create, read the warning on every DELETE, and never put real credentials or tokens into a shared or exported file.

_Restful Booker was created by Mark Winteringham. This learning collection is an independent community resource and isn't affiliated with the API's author._

item.name: 00 - Introduction and Health Check
item.description:
# Start here

Welcome to a **manual** API testing course built on the public Restful Booker API. Every request in this collection is a test case. Its **Docs** tab tells you what it does, what to enter, how to run it, what to inspect, what to expect and what to record.

## 1. One-time setup

1. Import `Restful-Booker-Manual-API-Testing.postman_collection.json` and `Restful-Booker-Environment.postman_environment.json` (**Import** button, top left).
2. Select **Restful Booker Environment** in the environment selector (top right of Postman).
3. Open **Environments → Restful Booker Environment** and check the variables:

| Variable | Starts as | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| `base_url` | `https://restful-booker.herokuapp.com` | Base URL used by every request |
| `username` | `admin` | Documented public demo username |
| `password` | `password123` | Documented public demo password |
| `booking_id` | _empty_ | You paste the ID of a booking **you** created |
| `token` | _empty_ | You paste the token returned by `POST /auth` |

4. Run **00.01** below. If it returns `201 Created`, you're ready.

## 2. How to read each request

- **Docs tab** of a request: the full test case (ID, scenario, preconditions, test data, steps, expected result, common mistakes, fields to record).
- **Overview tab** of a folder: the theory for that chapter and the execution order.
- **Params / Authorization / Headers / Body** tabs: the request itself. Every header, query parameter and path variable has a description explaining its purpose.

## 3. Golden rules

1. **Manual only.** This collection contains no scripts, no automatic assertions and no automatic variable extraction. Leave the **Scripts** tab empty. You run each request, inspect the response and update the environment yourself.
2. **Only change or delete bookings you created.** Other people use this API at the same time.
3. **Read the warning** on every DELETE request before sending it.
4. **Don't save experiments.** If you change a request to try something, don't click Save, or duplicate the request first.
5. **Record every result** (actual status code, actual result, Pass/Fail/Blocked, notes/defect ID) in `Test-Execution-Report-Template.md`.
6. **Use fresh IDs.** The API resets periodically and restarts its ID counter, so an old `booking_id` may now point to someone else's booking, even one that looks identical to yours. Create a fresh practice booking (**18.01**) at the start of each folder and after any break. Before a PUT, PATCH or DELETE on an older booking, GET it and check that it still shows the changes you made.

## 4. Things to know about this public API

- It is **shared**: data can be created, changed or deleted by others at any time.
- The Restful Booker home page states that it **resets to its default data every 10 minutes**. Bookings and tokens you created may disappear, and IDs may be reused. Re-create test data with folder **18** when that happens.
- It is a practice API that is **deliberately loaded with bugs**. Finding and reporting them is part of the exercise.
- The first request after a quiet period can be slow.

## 5. How expected results are written

- **Documented:** the official documentation (https://restful-booker.herokuapp.com/apidoc/index.html) describes the behaviour. If the API behaves differently, the test fails.
- **Not documented - investigate:** the documentation is silent, so the test states the common HTTP convention and the acceptance criteria to judge against. Record exactly what you observe.
- **Mentor notes** at the bottom of some requests describe what the author observed on a local build of the official restful-booker source (commit 0046115, March 2026). Read them only after recording your own result. The public instance may behave differently, and **your observation is what counts**.

## 6. Test case ID scheme

`RB-<AREA>-<NNN>`, for example `RB-GET-001`. Areas: HC health check, FUND fundamentals, GET/POST/PUT/PATCH/DEL HTTP methods, STAT status codes, HDR headers, PARAM parameters, JSON request body, AUTH authentication, AUTHZ authorization, CON contracts, POS positive, NEG negative, BND boundary, BIZ business validation, TCD test case design, CHAIN chaining, CRUD workflow, E2E end-to-end, UTIL reusable/cleanup.

## 7. Suggested path

Work through folders **00 → 18** in order, running requests in their numbered order. Folders 16 (CRUD) and 17 (End-to-End) are self-contained, so you can repeat them at any time.

item.name: 00.01 [RB-HC-001] Health check - API is up (GET /ping)

request.description:
**Test Case ID:** `RB-HC-001` · **Priority:** High · **Type:** Positive  
**Concept:** Health check: confirming the system under test is available before testing

### What this request does

Sends `GET /ping`, the documented health-check endpoint. A quick check that the API is reachable before you start any other test. If this fails, every other result is unreliable.

### Test case

- **Test scenario:** Verify that the Restful Booker API is up and responding.
- **Preconditions:** Collection and environment imported; **Restful Booker Environment** selected.
- **Test data:** None. No parameters, headers or body.

### What you need to enter

Nothing. The URL is built from `{{base_url}}` in the environment.

### Steps

1. Check that **Restful Booker Environment** is selected in the environment selector (top right of Postman).
2. Hover over `{{base_url}}` in the URL bar. It should show `https://restful-booker.herokuapp.com`.
3. Click **Send**.
4. Read the status line above the response: status code, status text, time and size.
5. Open the response **Body** and **Headers** tabs.

### What to inspect

- Status code and status text.
- Body: a short plain-text word, not JSON.
- Response header `Content-Type`.
- Response time: the first call after a quiet period may take a few seconds.

### Expected result

- **Expected status code:** `201 Created`
- **Reason:** The documented HealthCheck response is `HTTP/1.1 201 Created`.
- **Expected behaviour:** The API answers quickly with 201 and a short plain-text body.
- **Source of the expectation:** Documented (HealthCheck).
- **Mark as Pass if:** The status is `201 Created`.
- **Mark as Fail if:** Any other status code. If the API can't be reached at all (timeout, DNS or network error), mark the test **Blocked**, not Fail, and retry later.

### Common mistakes

- No environment selected: `{{base_url}}` stays unresolved (shown in red) and the request never reaches the API.
- Expecting `200 OK` because 'GET normally returns 200'. Always compare with the documentation, not your assumptions.
- Typing the URL by hand and adding a typo such as `/pings` or a trailing space.

### Record your result

Copy these into your execution report (`Test-Execution-Report-Template.md`): status code and key facts go in **Actual Result**, the status in **Pass/Fail/Blocked**, any defect ID in **Defect ID**, and everything else in **Remarks**.

| Field | Your entry |
|---|---|
| Actual status code | _Fill in manually_ |
| Actual result | _Fill in manually_ |
| Status (Pass / Fail / Blocked) | _Fill in manually_ |
| Notes / Defect ID | _Fill in manually_ |

### Mentor note (read after you record your result)

A `201 Created` for a GET is unusual API design (201 normally means a resource was created), but it is documented, so this test passes. You can note it as a design observation. Reference build: `201 Created`, body `Created`, `Content-Type: text/plain; charset=utf-8`.

item.name: 01 - API Fundamentals and Request Anatomy
item.description:
# API fundamentals and request anatomy

## Key ideas

- **API (Application Programming Interface):** a contract that lets one program (the **client**, here Postman) ask another program (the **server**, here Restful Booker) to do something.
- **Client-server communication:** the client sends a **request** over HTTP(S). The server processes it and returns a **response**. Each request is independent: the server doesn't remember earlier requests unless you send something (like a token) that identifies you.
- **Base URL:** the common root of every request: `https://restful-booker.herokuapp.com` (stored in `{{base_url}}`).
- **Endpoint:** a specific path on the server, for example `/booking` or `/auth`.
- **Resource:** the thing an endpoint represents. `/booking` is the collection of bookings; `/booking/42` is one booking.
- **HTTP method:** the action to perform (GET read, POST create, PUT replace, PATCH partially update, DELETE remove).

## Anatomy of a request

```
PATCH https://restful-booker.herokuapp.com/booking/42?optional=query   <- method + URL (base URL + endpoint + path parameter + query)
Content-Type: application/json                                       <- headers
Accept: application/json
Authorization: Basic YWRtaW4...                                      <- authentication credentials
                                                                       (blank line)
{ "additionalneeds": "Late checkout" }                               <- body
```

## Anatomy of a response

Status line (`200 OK`), response headers (`Content-Type`, `Content-Length`, ...) and an optional body (JSON, XML or text).

## Where you'll see each part in this folder

| Part | Request |
|---|---|
| Method, base URL, endpoint, response inspection | 01.01 |
| Query parameters (tick/untick in Params) | 01.01 |
| Headers and JSON body | 01.02 |
| Path parameter, authentication credentials, the raw request in the Console | 01.03 |

## Execution order

01.01 → 01.02 (**save `booking_id`**) → 01.03.

item.name: 01.01 [RB-FUND-001] Your first request - list all booking IDs (GET /booking)

OPTIONAL filter (documented): return bookings with this last name. Unticked on purpose.

request.description:
**Test Case ID:** `RB-FUND-001` · **Priority:** High · **Type:** Positive  
**Concept:** API fundamentals: base URL, endpoint, resource, HTTP method, client-server request and response

### What this request does

Asks the server for the IDs of all bookings. It's the simplest booking request: one method, one URL, no body, no authentication.

### Test case

- **Test scenario:** Retrieve the list of booking IDs and identify every part of the request and the response.
- **Preconditions:** Collection and environment imported; **Restful Booker Environment** selected.
- **Test data:** None. Two optional query parameters (`firstname`, `lastname`) appear in **Params** but are unticked (disabled).

### What you need to enter

Nothing to run the test. For the anatomy exercise in step 6 you'll tick and untick a query parameter.

### Steps

1. Check that **Restful Booker Environment** is selected in the environment selector (top right of Postman).
2. Identify the parts of the URL: base URL `{{base_url}}` (https://restful-booker.herokuapp.com) + endpoint `/booking`. The resource is *booking*; the method is **GET**.
3. Click **Send**.
4. Read the status line above the response: status code, status text, time and size.
5. Open the response **Body** (Pretty view). You get a JSON **array** of objects, each with a `bookingid`.
6. Anatomy exercise: in **Params**, tick `firstname` and watch the URL change to `...?firstname=Asha`. Untick it again so the request lists all IDs. Filtering is practised in folder 05.

### What to inspect

- Status `200 OK`, response time and size.
- Body: an array like `[{"bookingid": 1}, {"bookingid": 7}, ...]`. Each item has only a numeric `bookingid`.
- Response header `Content-Type` (expect JSON).
- How many bookings exist right now? Run it again in a few minutes and compare. This is a shared, resetting API.

### Expected result

- **Expected status code:** `200 OK`
- **Reason:** Documented response for GetBookingIds.
- **Expected behaviour:** A JSON array of objects that contain unique booking IDs. The IDs change constantly because the API is shared and resets periodically.
- **Source of the expectation:** Documented (GetBookingIds).
- **Mark as Pass if:** `200 OK` and the body is a JSON array of objects, each with a numeric `bookingid`.
- **Mark as Fail if:** Any other status, or a body that isn't an array of `{ "bookingid": <number> }` objects.

### Common mistakes

- No environment selected: `{{base_url}}` stays unresolved (shown in red) and the request never reaches the API.
- Expecting the same IDs as the documentation example (1, 2, 3, 4) or as yesterday. IDs aren't fixed.
- Leaving a query parameter ticked by accident: the result is then filtered.
- Editing the request (for example the body) and then clicking **Save** - that permanently changes the collection. Experiment freely, but don't save, or duplicate the request first.

### Record your result

Copy these into your execution report (`Test-Execution-Report-Template.md`): status code and key facts go in **Actual Result**, the status in **Pass/Fail/Blocked**, any defect ID in **Defect ID**, and everything else in **Remarks**.

| Field | Your entry |
|---|---|
| Actual status code | _Fill in manually_ |
| Actual result | _Fill in manually_ |
| Status (Pass / Fail / Blocked) | _Fill in manually_ |
| Notes / Defect ID | _Fill in manually_ |

### Mentor note (read after you record your result)

Client-server in one sentence: Postman sends `GET /booking` over HTTPS, the server looks up its data and answers with a status line, headers and a body. Every request in this course follows that cycle. Reference build: `200 OK`, `Content-Type: application/json; charset=utf-8`.

item.name: 01.02 [RB-FUND-002] Request anatomy - create your practice booking (POST /booking)

header.description: Format of the request body you are sending (documented: application/json or text/xml).
Response format you want back. Documented values: application/json or application/xml.

request.description:
**Test Case ID:** `RB-FUND-002` · **Priority:** High · **Type:** Positive  
**Concept:** Request anatomy: method + URL + headers + JSON body; first manual chaining step (save the ID)

### What this request does

Creates a new booking: **your practice booking**, used by many later requests. It shows the anatomy of a request that sends data: method, URL, headers and a JSON body. Afterwards you save the returned ID in the environment.

### Test case

- **Test scenario:** Create a booking with valid data and save its ID for later requests.
- **Preconditions:** Collection and environment imported; **Restful Booker Environment** selected.
- **Test data:** Body: firstname `Asha`, lastname `Verma`, totalprice `4500`, depositpaid `true`, checkin `2027-01-15`, checkout `2027-01-20`, additionalneeds `Breakfast` (the standard practice data).

### What you need to enter

Nothing before sending. **After** sending, copy the returned `bookingid` into the `booking_id` environment variable (steps 6-8).

### Steps

1. Check that **Restful Booker Environment** is selected in the environment selector (top right of Postman).
2. Method **POST**, URL `{{base_url}}/booking`. POST sends new data to the *collection* resource.
3. Open **Headers** and read the purpose of each header in the Description column.
4. Open **Body** (raw → JSON) and read the payload before sending. Notice the JSON data types: strings in double quotes, numbers without quotes, `true` without quotes, and `bookingdates` as a nested object.
5. Click **Send**.
6. In the response, find `bookingid` (top level, a number). Select only the number and copy it.
7. Open **Environments** (left sidebar) → **Restful Booker Environment** and paste the number as the value of `booking_id`. Depending on your Postman version the column is called *Value*, *Local value* or *Current value*. Recent versions save automatically; in older versions press **Ctrl/Cmd + S**.
8. Alternative manual method: select the number in the response, right-click → **Set as variable** → choose `booking_id`.
9. Hover over `{{booking_id}}` in request 01.03 to confirm it now resolves to your ID.

### What to inspect

- Status `200 OK`.
- Body: a top-level `bookingid` (number) and a `booking` object that echoes the data you sent.
- Each echoed value has the same data type as in the request (string, number, boolean, nested object).
- Response header `Content-Type`.

### Expected result

- **Expected status code:** `200 OK`
- **Reason:** Documented response for CreateBooking. Note that the documentation specifies 200, not the 201 that many APIs use for creation.
- **Expected behaviour:** The response contains a new numeric `bookingid` and a `booking` object whose values equal the request body.
- **Source of the expectation:** Documented (CreateBooking).
- **Mark as Pass if:** `200 OK`, a numeric `bookingid`, and every field in `booking` equals the value you sent.
- **Mark as Fail if:** Any other status, no `bookingid`, or any echoed field differs from the request.

### Common mistakes

- Copying the quotes or the whole JSON instead of just the number.
- Sending twice: each send creates another booking. That's harmless, just save the latest ID.
- Forgetting to save `booking_id`. Later requests then call `/booking/` or a wrong ID.
- Editing the request (for example the body) and then clicking **Save** - that permanently changes the collection. Experiment freely, but don't save, or duplicate the request first.

### Record your result

Copy these into your execution report (`Test-Execution-Report-Template.md`): status code and key facts go in **Actual Result**, the status in **Pass/Fail/Blocked**, any defect ID in **Defect ID**, and everything else in **Remarks**.

| Field | Your entry |
|---|---|
| Actual status code | _Fill in manually_ |
| Actual result | _Fill in manually_ |
| Status (Pass / Fail / Blocked) | _Fill in manually_ |
| Notes / Defect ID | _Fill in manually_ |

### Mentor note (read after you record your result)

This is your first **manual API chain**: the output of one request (`bookingid`) becomes the input of the next (`{{booking_id}}`). Folder 15 explores chaining in depth. You can recreate this practice booking at any time with **18.01**.

Response format you want back. Documented values: application/json or application/xml.

request.description:
**Test Case ID:** `RB-FUND-003` · **Priority:** High · **Type:** Positive  
**Concept:** Request anatomy: path parameter, headers, body and authentication credentials; inspecting the raw HTTP request

### What this request does

Partially updates your practice booking. This request has every part of a request at once: method, URL, path parameter, headers, authentication and body. You'll also see the raw HTTP request that Postman sends.

### Test case

- **Test scenario:** Send an authenticated partial update and inspect the complete HTTP request and response.
- **Preconditions:** Collection and environment imported; **Restful Booker Environment** selected. `booking_id` holds the ID of a booking **you** created (01.02 or 18.01) that still exists.
- **Test data:** Path `id` = `{{booking_id}}`. Basic Auth from `{{username}}` / `{{password}}`. Body: `{"additionalneeds": "Breakfast and late checkout"}`.

### What you need to enter

Nothing. All values come from the environment.

### Steps

1. Check that **Restful Booker Environment** is selected in the environment selector (top right of Postman).
2. Walk through the tabs: **Params** (path variable `id`), **Authorization** (Basic Auth), **Headers**, **Body**.
3. Click **Send**.
4. Open the **Postman Console** (Console button in the bottom status bar, or View → Show Postman Console). Expand the PATCH entry and read the **Request Headers**: find the `Authorization: Basic ...` header that Postman generated from the Authorization tab, plus auto-generated headers such as `User-Agent`, `Accept` and `Content-Length`.
5. Optional: open the **Code** panel (`</>` icon) and choose cURL to see the same request as a command.

### What to inspect

- Status `200 OK`.
- Body: the full booking. `additionalneeds` changed and every other field is unchanged.
- In the Console: method, full URL with your ID, request headers and request body, then the response headers and body.

### Expected result

- **Expected status code:** `200 OK`
- **Reason:** Documented response for PartialUpdateBooking.
- **Expected behaviour:** The full booking is returned; only `additionalneeds` has changed.
- **Source of the expectation:** Documented (PartialUpdateBooking).
- **Mark as Pass if:** `200 OK`, `additionalneeds` = `Breakfast and late checkout`, and all other fields unchanged.
- **Mark as Fail if:** Any other status, or any field other than `additionalneeds` changed.

### Common mistakes

- `booking_id` is empty: the URL becomes `/booking/`. For GET that's a different endpoint (it lists bookings); for PUT, PATCH and DELETE no route matches. Set the variable first.
- Your booking no longer exists (periodic API reset or deleted by someone else) → `404`/`405`. Create a new one with **18.01** and update `booking_id`.
- Sharing a Console screenshot that shows credentials. Basic Auth is only Base64-encoded, not encrypted, so anyone can decode it. These are public demo credentials, but on real projects treat them as secrets.

### Record your result

Copy these into your execution report (`Test-Execution-Report-Template.md`): status code and key facts go in **Actual Result**, the status in **Pass/Fail/Blocked**, any defect ID in **Defect ID**, and everything else in **Remarks**.

| Field | Your entry |
|---|---|
| Actual status code | _Fill in manually_ |
| Actual result | _Fill in manually_ |
| Status (Pass / Fail / Blocked) | _Fill in manually_ |
| Notes / Defect ID | _Fill in manually_ |

### Mentor note (read after you record your result)

Anatomy checklist you just saw: **Method** PATCH · **URL** = base URL + `/booking/` + **path parameter** · **Headers** Content-Type, Accept, Authorization (plus auto-generated ones) · **Body** JSON · **Credentials** Basic Auth. The only part not used here is the **query parameter**: you saw it in 01.01 and you'll practise it in folder 05.

item.name: 02 - HTTP Methods
item.description:
# HTTP methods

| Method | Purpose | Safe? | Idempotent? | Restful Booker endpoint | Documented success |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| GET | Read a resource | Yes | Yes | `GET /booking`, `GET /booking/:id` | 200 OK |
| POST | Create a resource | No | No | `POST /booking` (also `POST /auth`) | 200 OK |
| PUT | Replace a resource completely | No | Yes | `PUT /booking/:id` | 200 OK |
| PATCH | Update part of a resource | No | Not guaranteed | `PATCH /booking/:id` | 200 OK |
| DELETE | Remove a resource | No | Yes | `DELETE /booking/:id` | 201 Created |

- **Safe:** doesn't change server data.
- **Idempotent:** sending the same request once or many times leaves the server in the same state.
- These are properties defined by the HTTP standard (RFC 9110). The success codes in the last column come from the Restful Booker documentation.

## Full update (PUT) vs partial update (PATCH)

- **PUT** sends the **whole** booking. Every documented field is required.
- **PATCH** sends **only the fields to change**. Every field is optional.
- Requests 02.03 → 02.05 compare them directly.

## Authentication in this folder

PUT, PATCH and DELETE need credentials. To keep the focus on methods, these requests use the documented **Basic Auth** alternative, already configured in the **Authorization** tab from `{{username}}`/`{{password}}`. Tokens are covered in folders 07 and 08.

## Execution order and state

02.01 → 02.02 → 02.03 → 02.04 → 02.05 → **02.06 (deletes your practice booking)** → 02.07.

**After 02.07, run 18.01 to create a new practice booking and save its ID before starting folder 03.**

item.name: 02.01 [RB-GET-001] GET - retrieve your booking (safe and idempotent)

header.description: Response format you want back. Documented values: application/json or application/xml.

variable.description: PATH PARAMETER: ID of the booking to retrieve (from the environment).

request.description:
**Test Case ID:** `RB-GET-001` · **Priority:** High · **Type:** Positive  
**Concept:** HTTP methods: GET reads data without changing it (safe) and gives the same result when repeated (idempotent)

### What this request does

Retrieves your practice booking by its ID. GET must not change data, and repeating it must return the same result.

### Test case

- **Test scenario:** Retrieve an existing booking and confirm that repeated GETs return identical data.
- **Preconditions:** Collection and environment imported; **Restful Booker Environment** selected. `booking_id` holds the ID of a booking **you** created (01.02 or 18.01) that still exists.
- **Test data:** Path `id` = `{{booking_id}}`; header `Accept: application/json`.

### What you need to enter

Nothing.

### Steps

1. Check that **Restful Booker Environment** is selected in the environment selector (top right of Postman).
2. Open **Params** → **Path Variables**: `id` = `{{booking_id}}`. Hover over `{{booking_id}}` to confirm it resolves to your booking ID.
3. Click **Send**.
4. Read the status line above the response: status code, status text, time and size.
5. Send the request two more times and compare the bodies.
6. Compare the response time of each send.

### What to inspect

- Status `200 OK`.
- Fields: `firstname`, `lastname`, `totalprice`, `depositpaid`, `bookingdates.checkin`, `bookingdates.checkout`, `additionalneeds`.
- Values match the data you created (`additionalneeds` was changed by 01.03).
- The three responses are identical.

### Expected result

- **Expected status code:** `200 OK`
- **Reason:** Documented response for GetBooking.
- **Expected behaviour:** Returns the booking as JSON; repeating the request returns the same data and changes nothing.
- **Source of the expectation:** Documented (GetBooking). Safety and idempotency are properties of the GET method (RFC 9110).
- **Mark as Pass if:** `200 OK` every time, the data matches your booking, and repeated responses are identical.
- **Mark as Fail if:** Any other status, wrong data, or responses that differ between sends when nobody changed the booking.

### Common mistakes

- `booking_id` is empty: the URL becomes `/booking/`. For GET that's a different endpoint (it lists bookings); for PUT, PATCH and DELETE no route matches. Set the variable first.
- Your booking no longer exists (periodic API reset or deleted by someone else) → `404`/`405`. Create a new one with **18.01** and update `booking_id`.
- Removing the `Accept` header. Folder 04 shows what happens then.

### Record your result

Copy these into your execution report (`Test-Execution-Report-Template.md`): status code and key facts go in **Actual Result**, the status in **Pass/Fail/Blocked**, any defect ID in **Defect ID**, and everything else in **Remarks**.

| Field | Your entry |
|---|---|
| Actual status code | _Fill in manually_ |
| Actual result | _Fill in manually_ |
| Status (Pass / Fail / Blocked) | _Fill in manually_ |
| Notes / Defect ID | _Fill in manually_ |

### Mentor note (read after you record your result)

**Concept:** HTTP methods: POST creates a new resource and is not idempotent

### What this request does

Creates a new booking. POST is neither safe nor idempotent: each send creates another resource with a new ID.

### Test case

- **Test scenario:** Send the same POST twice and confirm that two separate bookings are created.
- **Preconditions:** Collection and environment imported; **Restful Booker Environment** selected.
- **Test data:** Body: Rahul Nair, totalprice `3200`, depositpaid `false`, 2027-02-10 → 2027-02-12, additionalneeds `Airport pickup`.

3. Click **Send**.
4. Write down the returned `bookingid`.
5. Click **Send** again and write down the new `bookingid`.

- Two **different** `bookingid` values.

**Test Case ID:** `RB-PUT-002` · **Priority:** High · **Type:** Negative  
**Concept:** HTTP methods: comparing full updates (PUT) with partial updates (PATCH)

### What this request does

Sends a one-field body like 02.04 (with a new price, 5800), but with **PUT**, to compare how the API treats an incomplete full update.

### Test case

- **Test scenario:** A PUT with an incomplete body must not be accepted as a full update.
- **Preconditions:** Collection and environment imported; **Restful Booker Environment** selected. `booking_id` holds the ID of a booking **you** created (01.02 or 18.01) that still exists. Run 02.04 first (the current price is 5600).
- **Test data:** Body: `{"totalprice": 5800}` only. Every other documented field is missing. A different price from 02.04 lets you see whether anything changed.

### What you need to enter

Nothing.

### Steps

1. Check that **Restful Booker Environment** is selected in the environment selector (top right of Postman).
2. Open **Params** → **Path Variables**: `id` = `{{booking_id}}`. Hover over `{{booking_id}}` to confirm it resolves to your booking ID.
3. Open **Authorization**: Auth Type = **Basic Auth**, Username `{{username}}`, Password `{{password}}`. Postman turns these into an `Authorization: Basic ...` header when you send.
4. Open **Body** (raw → JSON) and read the payload before sending.
5. Click **Send**.
6. Read the status line above the response: status code, status text, time and size.
7. Then send **02.01** to verify that the booking didn't change.

### What to inspect

- Status code and status text.
- Response body: is there an error message explaining what's missing?
- The booking afterwards (02.01): is `totalprice` still 5600 and are the other fields intact?

### Expected result

- **Expected status code:** A `4xx` client error, most likely `400 Bad Request`.
- **Reason:** UpdateBooking documents every body field as required (none is marked optional), so an incomplete PUT should be rejected. The documentation doesn't specify the error code.
- **Expected behaviour:** The request is rejected and the booking stays unchanged.
- **Source of the expectation:** Partly documented: required fields are documented, the error response is not. Investigate.
- **Mark as Pass if:** A 4xx status and the booking is unchanged (verify with 02.01).
- **Mark as Fail if:** 2xx (incomplete PUT accepted), any 5xx, or the booking changed.
- **Defect or observation?** Part of this expectation isn't documented. If the only deviation is from an HTTP convention (for example a different 4xx code, or 200 with an error body), log it as an **observation** (report section 6). Raise a **defect** for server errors (5xx), changed or lost data, or access without valid credentials.

### Common mistakes

- Expecting PUT to behave like PATCH. They're different methods with different contracts.
- Skipping the follow-up GET. A rejected request must also leave the data unchanged.

item.name: 03 - Status Codes
item.description:
# Status codes

The status code is the server's one-line verdict on your request. Always record it, but never judge a test by the status code alone: read the body and headers too.

| Class | Meaning | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| 1xx | Informational | rarely seen in API testing |
| 2xx | Success | 200 OK, 201 Created, 204 No Content |
| 3xx | Redirection | 301, 302, 304 |
| 4xx | Client error: the request is wrong | 400 Bad Request, 401 Unauthorized, 403 Forbidden, 404 Not Found, 405 Method Not Allowed, 406 Not Acceptable, 415 Unsupported Media Type, 418 I'm a Teapot |
| 5xx | Server error: the server failed | 500 Internal Server Error, 503 Service Unavailable |

## What the Restful Booker documentation specifies

Only **success** responses: `200 OK` for auth, list, get, create, update and partial update, and `201 Created` for ping and delete. **No error responses are documented**, so every error-code test here is *Investigate*: compare against HTTP conventions and record what you observe.

## Status code map for this collection

| Status | Where you meet it first |
|---|---|
| 200 OK | 01.01, 02.01 |
| 201 Created | 00.01 (ping), 02.06 (delete) |
| 4xx for a missing booking | 02.07, 03.01, 03.02 |
| 4xx/5xx for bad input | 02.05, 03.04, 03.05, folders 06 and 11 |
| 4xx for missing or invalid credentials | 03.03, folder 08 |
| Unusual codes such as 418 | folder 04 |

## For every request, record

1. Expected status code (from the Docs tab)
2. Actual status code **and** status text
3. Reason for the response (what in the request caused it?)
4. Pass / Fail / Blocked

## Precondition for this folder

A fresh practice booking in `booking_id` (run **18.01** after finishing folder 02).

item.name: 04 - Headers and Content Types
item.description:
# Headers and content types

Headers are key-value metadata sent with requests and responses.

| Header | Direction | Meaning | Documented for |
|---|---|---|---|
| `Content-Type` | request | Format of the body **you send** | POST /auth (application/json), POST/PUT/PATCH /booking (application/json or text/xml) |
| `Accept` | request | Format you want **back** | GET /booking/:id, POST/PUT/PATCH /booking (application/json or application/xml) |
| `Cookie` | request | Carries `token=<value>` | PUT, PATCH, DELETE /booking/:id |
| `Authorization` | request | `Basic <base64 username:password>` | PUT, PATCH, DELETE /booking/:id |
| `Content-Type` | response | Format of the body you **received** | (should match the body) |

## Headers Postman adds for you

Postman auto-generates headers such as `User-Agent`, `Accept: */*`, `Accept-Encoding`, `Connection`, `Postman-Token`, and (when there's a body) `Content-Type` and `Content-Length`. Open **Headers → hidden** (or the eye icon) to see them. A header you add yourself replaces the auto-generated one with the same name. You can also untick an auto-generated header so it isn't sent. Requests 04.02 and 04.04 already have one unticked.

## Not every endpoint treats headers the same way

- `GET /booking` (list) documents no headers.
- `GET /booking/:id` documents `Accept`.
- `POST /auth` documents only `Content-Type`.

Don't assume one endpoint's behaviour applies to another. Test each one.

## Execution order

04.01 → 04.02 → 04.03 → 04.04 → 04.05 → 04.06 (verifies 04.05).

Precondition: a practice booking in `booking_id`.

**Tip:** on a shared API other learners may use the same test-data marker (`RB-HDR-005`). For an unambiguous result, change the lastname in 04.05 **and** 04.06 to something unique, such as `RB-HDR-005-<your initials>`.

item.name: 04.01 [RB-HDR-001] Accept: application/xml - ask for XML instead of JSON

request.description:
**Test Case ID:** `RB-HDR-001` · **Priority:** Medium · **Type:** Positive  
**Concept:** Headers: the Accept header and content negotiation

### What this request does

Asks for your booking in XML instead of JSON. Choosing the response format with the Accept header is called content negotiation.

### Test case

- **Test scenario:** Retrieve a booking in the documented alternative format (XML).
- **Preconditions:** Collection and environment imported; **Restful Booker Environment** selected. `booking_id` holds the ID of a booking **you** created (01.02 or 18.01) that still exists.
- **Test data:** Header `Accept: application/xml`.

### What you need to enter

Nothing.

### Steps

1. Check that **Restful Booker Environment** is selected in the environment selector (top right of Postman).
2. Open **Params** → **Path Variables**: `id` = `{{booking_id}}`. Hover over `{{booking_id}}` to confirm it resolves to your booking ID.
3. Open **Headers** and read the purpose of each header in the Description column.
4. Click **Send**.
5. Read the status line above the response: status code, status text, time and size.
6. Look at the body (it should be XML) and then at the response `Content-Type` header.
7. Compare the values with the JSON from 02.01 (send 02.01 again if needed).

### What to inspect

- Status `200 OK`.
- Body format: XML elements such as `<firstname>`.
- Values identical to the JSON representation.
- Response `Content-Type`: does it say XML?

### Expected result

- **Expected status code:** `200 OK`
- **Reason:** GetBooking documents `Accept: application/xml` and shows an XML response example.
- **Expected behaviour:** Documented: the booking is returned as XML with the same values as the JSON representation. Convention (RFC 9110, not documented): the response `Content-Type` should identify the body as XML.
- **Source of the expectation:** Partly documented (XML response documented; response headers aren't documented).
- **Mark as Pass if:** `200 OK` and an XML body with the correct values.
- **Mark as Fail if:** JSON or an error is returned, or values differ. Separately, if the response `Content-Type` doesn't describe the XML body, record that as an observation (the convention part).
- **Defect or observation?** Part of this expectation isn't documented. If the only deviation is from an HTTP convention (for example a different 4xx code, or 200 with an error body), log it as an **observation** (report section 6). Raise a **defect** for server errors (5xx), changed or lost data, or access without valid credentials.

### Common mistakes

- Adding a second `Accept` header instead of changing the existing one.
- Checking only the body and not the response headers.

### Record your result

Copy these into your execution report (`Test-Execution-Report-Template.md`): status code and key facts go in **Actual Result**, the status in **Pass/Fail/Blocked**, any defect ID in **Defect ID**, and everything else in **Remarks**.

| Field | Your entry |
|---|---|
| Actual status code | _Fill in manually_ |
| Actual result | _Fill in manually_ |
| Status (Pass / Fail / Blocked) | _Fill in manually_ |
| Notes / Defect ID | _Fill in manually_ |

### Mentor note (read after you record your result)

Reference build: `200 OK` with a correct XML body, but the response header says `Content-Type: text/html; charset=utf-8`. The body is XML while the header claims HTML. That's a contract defect: clients that trust Content-Type will mis-parse the response. It's why you always inspect headers, not just the body.

**Test Case ID:** `RB-HDR-002` · **Priority:** Medium · **Type:** Exploratory  
**Concept:** Headers: missing header and Postman's auto-generated headers

### What this request does

Sends the GET **without any Accept header**. Postman normally adds `Accept: */*` automatically, but that auto-generated header is unticked in this request.

### Test case

- **Test scenario:** Retrieve a booking when the client doesn't send an Accept header.
- **Preconditions:** Collection and environment imported; **Restful Booker Environment** selected. `booking_id` holds the ID of a booking **you** created (01.02 or 18.01) that still exists.
- **Test data:** No Accept header (auto-generated Accept disabled).

### What you need to enter

Nothing for the main test. Step 6 is an optional comparison.

### Steps

1. Check that **Restful Booker Environment** is selected in the environment selector (top right of Postman).
2. Open **Params** → **Path Variables**: `id` = `{{booking_id}}`. Hover over `{{booking_id}}` to confirm it resolves to your booking ID.
3. Open **Headers** and click **hidden** (or the eye icon) to show auto-generated headers. `Accept` is unticked, so Postman won't send it.
4. Click **Send**.
5. Read the status line above the response: status code, status text, time and size.
6. Optional comparison: tick the auto-generated `Accept` (`*/*`), send again and compare. Then untick it again, or don't save.

### What to inspect

- Status code and status text.
- Body: JSON booking, an error, or something else?
- In the Postman Console, confirm that no Accept header was sent.

### Expected result

- **Expected status code:** `200 OK` with the JSON booking, **or** a clear `400`/`406` saying the Accept header is required
- **Reason:** GetBooking lists `Accept` as a header with the default value `application/json` and doesn't mark it optional, so a server could either apply the default or reject the request. Under HTTP semantics (RFC 9110), no Accept header means 'any media type is acceptable'. What actually happens without it isn't documented.
- **Expected behaviour:** Either the default format (JSON) is returned, or the request is rejected with a standard status code that explains the problem.
- **Source of the expectation:** Partly documented (Accept listed with a default; behaviour without it not documented). Investigate.
- **Mark as Pass if:** `200 OK` with the booking, **or** a standard `400`/`406` with an explanation.
- **Mark as Fail if:** Any 5xx, a non-standard status code, or a success status without the booking.
- **Defect or observation?** Part of this expectation isn't documented. If the only deviation is from an HTTP convention (for example a different 4xx code, or 200 with an error body), log it as an **observation** (report section 6). Raise a **defect** for server errors (5xx), changed or lost data, or access without valid credentials.

### Common mistakes

- Deleting your own `Accept` header but leaving Postman's auto-generated one ticked. Then you're not testing a missing header.
- Editing the request (for example the body) and then clicking **Save** - that permanently changes the collection. Experiment freely, but don't save, or duplicate the request first.

### Record your result

Copy these into your execution report (`Test-Execution-Report-Template.md`): status code and key facts go in **Actual Result**, the status in **Pass/Fail/Blocked**, any defect ID in **Defect ID**, and everything else in **Remarks**.

|---|---|

| Actual result | _Fill in manually_ |
| Status (Pass / Fail / Blocked) | _Fill in manually_ |
| Notes / Defect ID | _Fill in manually_ |

### Mentor note (read after you record your result)

Reference build: `418 I'm a Teapot` without Accept, and also for `Accept: text/plain`, `Accept: application/json; charset=utf-8` and even the common browser value `application/json, text/plain, */*`. The server accepts only exact strings. With Postman's default `*/*` it returns JSON. 418 is a joke status code (from an April Fools' RFC), not a standard way to reject a request. Your report should include the exact header values you sent (the Console shows them).

item.name: 05 - Query and Path Parameters
item.description:
# Query and path parameters

| Kind | Where | Example | Purpose |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Path parameter** | inside the path | `/booking/:id` → `/booking/42` | Identifies **one** resource |
| **Query parameter** | after `?`, joined with `&` | `/booking?firstname=Asha&lastname=Verma` | Filters or modifies a **collection** request |

In Postman both live in the **Params** tab: *Query Params* (synced with the URL) and *Path Variables* (for `:name` segments). Each parameter in this collection has a description that explains its purpose.

## Documented query parameters for `GET /booking` (all optional)

| Parameter | Type | Documented meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `firstname` | String | Return bookings with a specific first name |
| `lastname` | String | Return bookings with a specific last name |
| `checkin` | date | Bookings with a check-in date **greater than or equal to** this date. Format must be **CCYY-MM-DD** |
| `checkout` | date | Bookings with a check-out date **greater than or equal to** this date. Format must be **CCYY-MM-DD** |

`bookingid` is **not** a documented query parameter. The booking ID is a **path** parameter of `GET/PUT/PATCH/DELETE /booking/:id`. Request 05.11 shows what happens if you use it as a query parameter anyway.

## Precondition: fresh practice booking with standard data

The filter tests assume your practice booking has the standard data: **Asha Verma, check-in 2027-01-15, check-out 2027-01-20**. Run **18.01** before this folder and save the ID.

## Path parameter tests across the collection

| Case | Request |
|---|---|
| Valid ID (your booking) | 02.01 |
| Non-existent ID | 03.01 |
| Missing ID | 05.12 |
| Malformed ID (digits followed by letters) | 05.13 |
| Non-numeric ID | 11.01 |
| Boundary IDs (0, very large) | 12.10, 12.11 |

item.name: 06 - JSON and Request Body
item.description:
# JSON and the request body

JSON has six value types: **string** (`"Asha"`), **number** (`4500`), **boolean** (`true`/`false`), **null**, **object** (`{ ... }`) and **array** (`[ ... ]`). Keys must be in double quotes, and items are separated by commas with no trailing comma.

## The booking schema (from the official documentation)

| Field | Type | POST /booking | PUT /booking/:id | PATCH /booking/:id |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `firstname` | String | required | required | optional |
| `lastname` | String | required | required | optional |
| `totalprice` | Number | required | required | optional |
| `depositpaid` | Boolean | required | required | optional |
| `bookingdates.checkin` | Date | required | required | optional |
| `bookingdates.checkout` | Date | required | required | optional |
| `additionalneeds` | String | required | required | optional |

- `bookingdates` is a **nested object** that contains `checkin` and `checkout`.
- The documentation's examples write dates as `YYYY-MM-DD` (the query parameters explicitly require CCYY-MM-DD).
- In apidoc, fields not marked as optional are required. In the official documentation **every** POST and PUT field, including `additionalneeds`, is marked required. Request 06.02 checks whether the API agrees.
- **Arrays:** the booking schema has no array fields, but `GET /booking` *returns* an array. Request 06.07 sends an array where an object is expected.

## Body settings in Postman

**Body → raw → JSON.** Postman colours the JSON and underlines syntax errors. **Beautify** re-formats valid JSON. Don't beautify the deliberately broken bodies.

## Execution order

06.01 → 06.08 (any order). Each test creates its own booking or none. Negative tests use lastnames such as `RB-JSON-004` so you can find any booking they create with a `lastname` filter.

item.name: 07 - Authentication
item.description:
# Authentication

**Authentication** answers *"who are you?"*. Restful Booker documents two ways to prove identity:

1. **Token (documented in CreateToken):** `POST /auth` with `{"username": "admin", "password": "password123"}` returns `{"token": "..."}`. You then send `Cookie: token=<value>` with PUT, PATCH and DELETE.
2. **Basic Auth (documented as an alternative):** send `Authorization: Basic <base64 of username:password>` with every protected request. In Postman: **Authorization → Basic Auth**.

The demo credentials `admin` / `password123` are published in the official documentation. They're **not secrets**. Never put real credentials into a public repository or an exported environment.

## Saving the token manually (no scripts)

1. Send **07.01**.
2. In the response, select only the token text (without the quotes) and copy it.
3. Open **Environments → Restful Booker Environment** and paste it as the value of `token` (column *Value*, *Local value* or *Current value*, depending on your Postman version). Prefer the local value: shared values sync to your Postman workspace.
4. Alternative manual method: select the token in the response → right-click → **Set as variable** → `token`.
5. Hover over `{{token}}` in request 08.01 to confirm it resolves.

## Tokens and the public API

The documentation doesn't say how long a token lasts. On the shared public instance, data and tokens may be cleared by the periodic reset. If a request that worked starts returning a 403, generate a new token (18.02).

## Authentication vs authorization

Authentication proves identity (this folder). Authorization decides what that identity may do (folder 08). The mentor note in 08.03 explains why the difference matters for status codes.

## Execution order

07.01 (**save `token`**) → 07.02 → 07.03 → 07.04 → 07.05.

item.name: 08 - Authorization
item.description:
# Authorization

| | Authentication | Authorization |
|---|---|---|
| Question | *Who are you?* | *What are you allowed to do?* |
| In Restful Booker | `POST /auth` checks username/password and issues a token | PUT, PATCH and DELETE check for a valid token **or** valid Basic Auth before changing data |
| Typical failure code | 401 Unauthorized | 403 Forbidden |

## Documented authorization mechanism (UpdateBooking, PartialUpdateBooking, DeleteBooking)

- `Cookie: token=<token_value>`: the token from `POST /auth`. **or**
- `Authorization: Basic YWRtaW46cGFzc3dvcmQxMjM=`: Base64 of `admin:password123`. In Postman use **Authorization → Basic Auth** with `{{username}}`/`{{password}}` instead of pasting the encoded string.
- `GET` and `POST /booking` need no credentials.

## Comparison matrix in this folder

All requests except 08.07 send the same harmless PATCH to **your** booking. Only the credentials differ:

| Request | Credentials sent |
|---|---|
| 08.01 | valid token in `Cookie` |
| 08.02 | valid Basic Auth |
| 08.03 | nothing |
| 08.04 | invalid token |
| 08.05 | malformed `Cookie` header |
| 08.06 | malformed `Authorization` header |
| 08.07 | DELETE with nothing (must be rejected) |

## Preconditions

A practice booking in `booking_id`, and a **fresh token** in `token` (07.01 or 18.02).

item.name: 09 - API Contracts and Response Validation
item.description:
# API contracts and manual response validation

An **API contract** is the documented agreement between client and server: endpoints, methods, inputs, response structure, field names, data types and status codes. Contract testing checks that responses keep that promise.

## Documented response contracts

| Endpoint | Structure |
|---|---|
| `GET /booking` | Array of objects; each object has `bookingid` (number) |
| `GET /booking/:id`, `PUT`, `PATCH` | Booking object (table below) |
| `POST /booking` | `{ "bookingid": Number, "booking": { ...booking object... } }` |
| `POST /auth` | `{ "token": String }` |

| Booking field | Documented type | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `firstname` | String | |
| `lastname` | String | |
| `totalprice` | Number | |
| `depositpaid` | Boolean | `true` / `false`, not strings |
| `bookingdates` | Object | contains `checkin` and `checkout` |
| `bookingdates.checkin` | Date | examples use `YYYY-MM-DD` |
| `bookingdates.checkout` | Date | examples use `YYYY-MM-DD` |
| `additionalneeds` | String | documented in responses; see 06.02 for its 'required' status |

## Manual validation checklist (use it for every response in this folder)

1. **Status code** and status text match the expectation.
2. **Response headers** *(convention; headers aren't documented)*: `Content-Type` matches the body (JSON → `application/json`). Note the charset.
3. **JSON structure:** object vs array, nesting, no unexpected wrapper.
4. **Required fields** are all present, with exact names (`firstname`, not `firstName`).
5. **No unexpected extra fields** *(convention)*.
6. **Data types:** numbers aren't quoted, booleans are `true`/`false`, objects are objects.
7. **Field values** equal what you sent or expect.
8. **Date formats:** `YYYY-MM-DD`, real calendar dates.
9. **Consistency:** the same booking looks identical in POST, GET, PUT and PATCH responses, and repeated GETs return the same data.
10. **Performance (informational):** note the response time.

This folder deliberately has **no Postman test scripts**. Tick the checklist by eye and record each deviation. Deviations from documented items are failures. Deviations from the *convention* items are observations.

## Preconditions

A practice booking with standard data (run **18.01**).

### Expected result

- **Expected status code:** `200 OK`

item.name: 10 - Positive Testing
item.description:
# Positive testing

Positive tests show that the API **does what it should with valid input**. Strong positive testing uses several *different* valid inputs (equivalence classes), not the same happy path repeated.

## Positive coverage across the collection

| Capability | Basic happy path | Positive variation in this folder |
|---|---|---|
| Authenticate | 07.01 | 10.01: repeated logins issue new tokens |
| Retrieve bookings | 01.01, 05.01-05.04 | 10.02: three documented filters combined |
| Retrieve an existing booking | 02.01 | 10.03: a booking you did **not** create (read-only) |
| Create a booking | 01.02, 06.01 | 10.04: valid special characters (hyphen, apostrophe, punctuation) |
| Update a booking (PUT) | 02.03 (Basic Auth) | 10.05: authorized with the **token** |
| Partially update (PATCH) | 02.04 (one field) | 10.06: several fields, including a complete nested object |
| Delete a booking | 02.06 (Basic Auth) | 10.07: authorized with the **token** |

## Preconditions

- A practice booking with standard data in `booking_id` (18.01) and a fresh `token` (07.01/18.02).
- 10.05 and 10.06 keep the guest name and check-in date unchanged so later filter tests still work.
- 10.07 deletes the booking created in **10.04**, not your practice booking.

## Execution order

10.01 → 10.07.

item.name: 11 - Negative Testing
item.description:
# Negative testing

Negative tests check that the API handles **invalid input and invalid conditions** gracefully:

1. it **rejects** the request with an appropriate **4xx** status (never a 5xx for client mistakes)
2. it **explains** the problem where possible
3. it causes **no side effects** (nothing created, changed or deleted)
4. it **leaks nothing sensitive** (no stack traces or internal details)

Restful Booker documents **no error responses**, so most expectations here are marked *Not documented - investigate*, judged against HTTP conventions and consistency. Always distinguish the **documented expected result** from the **observed result** you record.

## Negative coverage map

| Scenario | This folder | Related tests elsewhere |
|---|---|---|
| Invalid booking ID (format) | 11.01 | 05.13, 12.10, 12.11 |
| Non-existent booking ID | 11.02 | 03.01, 03.02, 14.01 |
| Invalid credentials | 11.03 | 07.02-07.05 |
| Missing required booking fields | 11.04 | 03.05, 06.02 |
| Incorrect data types | 11.05 | 06.04, 06.05, 06.06 |
| Malformed JSON | 11.06 | 03.04, 06.08 |
| Invalid or missing authentication | 11.07 | 03.03, 08.03-08.07 |
| Invalid headers | 11.08 | 04.02-04.05 |
| Unsupported method on a resource | 11.09 | |
| Wrong endpoint | 11.10 | |

## Preconditions

A practice booking in `booking_id` (for 11.06, 11.07 and 11.09) and a token in `token` (for 11.07). The other tests need nothing.

item.name: 12 - Boundary Testing
item.description:
# Boundary testing

**Boundary value analysis (BVA)** tests values at and around the edges of valid ranges, because defects cluster there (off-by-one errors, overflows, rounding). **Equivalence partitioning** picks one representative value from each class of input.

## What the documentation defines

- **No** numeric limits (minimum or maximum price, ID range).
- **No** string length limits.
- **No** business rules for dates (for example, check-out after check-in).
- **Only** the date *format* for query parameters (CCYY-MM-DD) and the date-filter semantics (**greater than or equal to**).

So almost everything here is **exploratory boundary testing**: choose natural edges, record exactly what was sent and what came back, and judge plausibility against the hotel-booking domain. Don't invent limits the API doesn't document. Report findings as *observations* or *questions* unless they contradict the documentation or clearly break the business meaning.

## Boundaries covered

| Area | Tests |
|---|---|
| `totalprice` | 12.01 zero · 12.02 negative · 12.03 decimals · 12.04 extremely large |
| Strings | 12.05 empty · 12.06 long (256 characters) |
| Missing fields | already covered: 03.05 (none), 06.02 (one optional-in-practice), 11.04 (required) |
| Dates and date ranges | 12.07 check-out before check-in · 12.08 invalid calendar date · 12.09 filter boundary (equal date) |
| Booking IDs | 12.10 zero · 12.11 very large (also 05.13 malformed and 11.01 non-numeric) |
| Optional fields | 12.12 empty `additionalneeds` |

Test data uses lastnames such as `RB-BND-003`, so you can find any booking a test creates with a `lastname` filter.

## Preconditions

None, except 12.09: it needs your practice booking with check-in **2027-01-15** (run 18.01 if unsure).

item.name: 13 - Business Validation
item.description:
# Business validation

Technical tests ask *"is the response well-formed?"*. Business validation asks *"does the system keep the hotel's data correct and meaningful?"*:

- Does the stored booking match what the guest submitted?
- Does an update change exactly the intended fields, and nothing else?
- Does a partial update preserve unrelated fields, including nested ones?
- Does 'replace' (PUT) really replace?
- Is a deleted booking gone everywhere (by ID and from search)?

The documentation describes the operations but **no business rules**. Where a rule is assumed (for example, 'PUT replaces the whole booking'), the test states the assumption and its source (HTTP semantics or documentation).

## This folder is a self-contained scenario

It creates its **own** booking (13.01), saves it in `booking_id`, and walks it through its life.

**Compare against what you SENT**, not against the previous response, because the response itself can be wrong.

| Step | Request | Business check |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | 13.01 | Create a booking (save `booking_id`) |
| 2 | 13.02 | Stored data = submitted data |
| 3 | 13.03 | PUT changes exactly the intended fields |
| 4 | 13.04 | PATCH preserves unrelated fields |
| 5 | 13.05 | PATCH of one nested date preserves the other date |
| 6 | 13.06 | PUT without `additionalneeds`: does 'replace' replace? |
| 7 | 13.07 | Delete (destructive) |
| 8 | 13.08 | Deleted booking not retrievable by ID |
| 9 | 13.09 | Deleted booking absent from search results |

After 13.09, `booking_id` points to a **deleted** booking. That's exactly the state 14.01 needs.

CRUD consistency as a whole is exercised in folder 16.

item.name: 14 - Test Case Design
item.description:
# Test case design

## What makes a good test case

- **One objective** (atomic): when it fails, you know why.
- **Explicit preconditions** and **exact test data**: anyone can repeat it.
- **Observable expected result** with its **source** (documentation, convention or business rule).
- **Independent**, or with clearly stated dependencies.
- **Traceable** to a requirement (an endpoint or a documented rule).
- **Prioritised:** High (core flow, security, data loss), Medium, Low.

Every request in this collection follows this template: Test Case ID, Scenario, Preconditions, Test Data, Steps, Expected Result, Actual Result, Status, Notes/Defect ID.

## Techniques with worked examples from this API

**1. Equivalence partitioning:** `depositpaid`

| Class | Example | Test |
|---|---|---|
| valid boolean | `true`, `false` | 01.02, 06.01 |
| string | `"false"` | 06.05 |
| number | `0` | 14.04 |
| null / missing | `null`, absent | your own extension |

**2. Boundary value analysis:** `totalprice` → -1, 0, decimals, huge (12.01-12.04); check-in filter edge (12.09).

**3. Decision table:** authorization for PATCH

| Rule | Cookie token | Basic Auth | Expected | Test |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| R1 | valid | none | allow | 08.01 |
| R2 | none | valid | allow | 08.02 |
| R3 | none | none | deny | 08.03 |
| R4 | invalid | none | deny | 08.04 |
| R5 | invalid | valid | *not documented* | **14.02** |
| R6 | valid | invalid | *not documented* | **14.03** |

**4. State transition:** booking life cycle

```
(none) --POST--> CREATED --PUT/PATCH--> UPDATED --DELETE--> DELETED
                    \---------------DELETE--------------------/
DELETED --PUT/PATCH/DELETE/GET--> must be refused (no resurrection)
```
Test: **14.01** (PATCH a deleted booking).

**5. Error guessing and exploratory testing:** wrong Content-Type (04.03), token in the URL (11.07), variable typos (15.05).

## Traceability (example)

| Requirement (documentation) | Tests |
|---|---|
| CreateBooking: all fields required | 01.02, 03.05, 06.02, 11.04 |
| GetBookingIds: checkin >= filter | 05.04, 10.02, 12.09 |
| PartialUpdateBooking: fields optional | 02.04, 10.06, 13.04, 13.05 |
| DeleteBooking: requires token or Basic Auth | 02.06, 08.07 |

## Execution order and state

14.01 uses the **deleted** booking left by folder 13. Then run **18.01** (fresh practice booking) and a fresh token (**18.02**) before 14.02-14.04.

item.name: 15 - API Chaining
item.description:
# API chaining (manual)

**Chaining** means using a value from one response as input to a later request. In automated suites a script does this. Here you do it **by hand**, which shows you exactly where each value comes from and goes to.

## The two values you chain in this API

| Value | Produced by | Copy from response | Paste into environment | Consumed by |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Booking ID | `POST /booking` | `bookingid` (top level) | `booking_id` | `GET/PUT/PATCH/DELETE /booking/{{booking_id}}` |
| Token | `POST /auth` | `token` | `token` | `Cookie: token={{token}}` on PUT/PATCH/DELETE |

## The 9-step booking chain: how the requests relate

| Step | Action | Consumes | Produces / changes | Your manual action | Folder 16 (Basic Auth) | Folder 17 (token) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | Get a token (token version only) | username, password | `token` | **copy → paste into `token`** | - | 17.02 |
| 1 | Create a booking | (nothing) | new `bookingid` | - | 16.01 | 17.03 |
| 2 | Record the booking ID | the `bookingid` in the response | `booking_id` in the environment | **copy → paste into `booking_id`** | 16.01 | 17.03 |
| 3 | Retrieve that booking | `booking_id` | - | compare with what you sent | 16.02 | 17.04 |
| 4 | Update it (PUT) | `booking_id` + credentials (Basic or `token`) | new field values | - | 16.03 | 17.05 |
| 5 | Retrieve again to verify | `booking_id` | - | compare with the PUT body | 16.04 | 17.06 |
| 6 | Partially update (PATCH) | `booking_id` + credentials | changed fields | - | 16.05 | 17.07 |
| 7 | Retrieve again | `booking_id` | - | check changed **and** preserved fields | 16.06 | 17.08 |
| 8 | Delete | `booking_id` + credentials | booking removed | read the warning first | 16.07 | 17.09 |
| 9 | Verify after deletion | `booking_id` | - | expect 'not found' | 16.08, 16.09 | 17.10 |

Folder **16** executes the chain with Basic Auth (only `booking_id` is chained). Folder **17** executes it with the token, so **both** `token` and `booking_id` are chained. This folder practises the individual **links** and what a **broken chain** looks like.

## When to copy and paste

- **Right after** a request that *produces* a value (POST /booking → `bookingid`, POST /auth → `token`), before you send anything that *consumes* it.
- **Again** whenever you create a new booking or token, because the old value is now stale.
- **After an API reset or a 403/404 you didn't expect:** recreate the value (folder 18) and paste it again.

## Typical chain breaks

| Symptom | Likely cause |
|---|---|
| URL shows `{{booking_id}}` in red, or the request goes to a literal `{{...}}` | variable name typo, or no environment selected |
| `GET /booking/{{booking_id}}` returns a **list** | `booking_id` is empty (see 05.12) |
| 404 for a booking you just created | wrong ID pasted, an extra space or quote, or API reset |
| 403 with a token you just saved | quotes pasted, `token=` missing in the Cookie, or token from before a reset |
| 'It worked yesterday' | values in the environment are stale; recreate them |

## Execution order

15.01 (**save `booking_id`**) → 15.02 → 15.03 (**save `token`**) → 15.04 → 15.05.

## Cleanup

After 15.05, `booking_id` still holds the Farhan Ali booking from 15.01. Delete it with **18.03**.

item.name: 16 - CRUD Workflow
item.description:
# CRUD workflow

**CRUD** = Create, Read, Update, Delete, the basic life cycle of any stored resource.

| CRUD | HTTP | Request(s) |
|---|---|---|
| Create | POST | 16.01 |
| Read | GET | 16.02, 16.04, 16.06, 16.08, 16.09 |
| Update (full) | PUT | 16.03 |
| Update (partial) | PATCH | 16.05 |
| Delete | DELETE | 16.07 |

This folder is **self-contained** and uses **one** booking ID from start to finish (the chain described in folder 15). PUT, PATCH and DELETE use **Basic Auth** (Authorization tab) so you can focus on the data life cycle. Folder 17 does the same with a token.

## Preconditions

- **Restful Booker Environment** selected; `username` and `password` set.
- Nothing else. 16.01 creates its own booking.

## Execution order (strict)

| # | Request | Manual action | Expected |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 16.01 Create | **copy `bookingid` → `booking_id`** | 200 |
| 2 | 16.02 Read | compare with the 16.01 body | 200 |
| 3 | 16.03 Update (PUT) | - | 200 |
| 4 | 16.04 Read | compare with the 16.03 body | 200 |
| 5 | 16.05 Partial update (PATCH) | - | 200 |
| 6 | 16.06 Read | changed and preserved fields | 200 |
| 7 | 16.07 Delete | read the warning | 201 |
| 8 | 16.08 Read deleted | - | 404 (convention) |
| 9 | 16.09 Search deleted | - | ID absent |

## Cleanup

16.07 deletes the booking. If you stop before 16.07, delete it later with **18.03**.

## Troubleshooting

- 404 at step 2-6: the ID is wrong or the API reset. Restart from 16.01.
- 403 at steps 3, 5 or 7: check the Authorization tab (Basic Auth, `{{username}}`/`{{password}}`).

item.name: 17 - End-to-End Booking Flow
item.description:
# End-to-end booking flow

A realistic guest journey, from 'is the system up?' to 'booking cancelled', using the **token** mechanism the way a real client application would.

## Life-cycle steps → requests

| Step | Life-cycle step | Request | Manual action |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Health check | 17.01 | stop if not 201 |
| 2 | Authenticate | 17.02 | **copy `token` → environment** |
| 3 | Create a booking | 17.03 | **copy `bookingid` → `booking_id`** |
| 4 | Retrieve the created booking | 17.04 | |
| 5 | Validate all important fields manually | 17.04 (validation table in its Docs tab) | |
| 6 | Update the booking | 17.05 | |
| 7 | Verify the updated values | 17.06 | |
| 8 | Partially update the booking | 17.07 | |
| 9 | Verify preserved and changed fields | 17.08 | |
| 10 | Delete the booking | 17.09 | read the warning |
| 11 | Verify deletion behaviour | 17.10 | |

Steps 4 and 5 use the same response, so they share one request rather than duplicating it.

## Preconditions

**Restful Booker Environment** selected; `username`/`password` set. The flow creates its own data. Run it without long pauses. If the API resets mid-flow (a sudden 404, or a 403 with a token you just saved), start again from 17.02.

## Cleanup

17.09 deletes the booking. If you stop early, delete it with **18.03** and clear `booking_id`/`token` afterwards (18.04).

## Troubleshooting

| Symptom | Fix |
|---|---|
| 17.01 fails or times out | Mark the run **Blocked**; retry later. |
| 403 on 17.05/17.07/17.09 | Re-run 17.02 and paste the token again (without quotes). Check `Cookie: token={{token}}`. |
| 404 on 17.04-17.08 | Wrong or stale `booking_id`, or the API reset. Restart from 17.03. |
| 17.04 shows different data | The ID was reused after a reset, or the paste was wrong. Restart from 17.03. |

item.name: 18 - Cleanup and Reusable Requests
item.description:
# Cleanup and reusable requests

Utility requests you can run at any time:

| Request | Use it when |
|---|---|
| **18.01** Create practice booking | You start a folder that needs a practice booking, or your booking was deleted or reset (any unexpected 404). |
| **18.02** Get a fresh token | You start token-based requests, or get an unexpected 403. |
| **18.03** Delete the current booking | You stopped a workflow early and want to remove your test booking. |
| **18.04** Verify cleanup and clear the environment | You've finished a session. |

## Good cleanup habits on a shared API

- Delete what you create when a flow is finished (16 and 17 do this themselves).
- Never delete or modify data you didn't create.
- Before exporting or committing anything, **clear `token` and `booking_id`** in the environment (Restful Booker Environment).
- The API also resets periodically, but don't rely on that as your cleanup strategy.
